The trombone is a **brass** instrument: the sound starts with your **lips buzzing** in a cup-shaped mouthpiece, like a trumpet. What makes it different
is that it has no valves to change the length of the tube. It has a **slide**, so you change the pitch by moving your right arm. That means a trombonist can play
every pitch in between the notes too, and has to **find each note by ear** as well as by position.

This page follows the **tenor trombone**, the one most beginners start on. The slide chart on this page is redrawn from the position charts in a teacher's
instrument guide (see the Works Cited), on the teacher's own drawing of the trombone.

## Where it came from {#history}

- The trombone has been the **tenor-baritone voice of the brass family** for roughly **600 years**. It comes from the **sackbut**, an older English name for the
  instrument, and first appears around the **middle of the 1400s**. It is believed to have been made first by **Flemish** craftsmen.
- It has changed **less** than most other brass instruments. The sackbut had a **much smaller bell flare**, so its tone was **softer and more supple**, and composers
  of its time liked it.
- Up to the 1600s it was mostly an **outdoor and church** instrument (masses and cantatas). In the Classical period it was used only a little, though Mozart and Beethoven
  did call for it in their masses.
- Makers built soprano, alto, tenor and bass versions, added **tuning slides** in the early 1800s, and sometimes **rotary valves** with extra tubing to reach lower notes.
- In the Romantic period it came back into favour, largely because **Beethoven used trombones in his symphonies**. Composers had written for an **alto, tenor and bass**
  trio; by the 1900s the band and orchestra normally used **tenor and bass**. The 1900s also brought new materials, mouthpieces, bore and bell sizes, and the
  option of a rotary valve with a tube extension.

## The trombone family {#family}

The book names four main members.

| Trombone | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Tenor** | The one people mean by "trombone". Beginners to professionals play it. A cylindrical tube, a bell 6 to 8½ inches across, a bore from 0.480 to 0.547 inches. **Not a transposing instrument** (it sounds as written). Usually read in **bass clef**; advanced players also read **tenor, alto and treble clef**. Many have a valve (see the F attachment below). |
| **Bass** | Looks very like the tenor. Bell about 9½ to 11½ inches, bore 0.562 inches, and a **much bigger mouthpiece**, which gives a darker tone, especially low down. Most have one or two valves. |
| **Alto** | Named in the book but not described in the pages used for this lesson. |
| **Valve trombone** | Named in the book but not described in the pages used for this lesson. |

## The parts {#parts}

**Bell section**

- **Bell**: the flared end the sound comes out of.
- **Bell brace**: the support bar between the bell tube and the slide. Your left thumb goes around it.
- **Tuning slide**: the U-bend at the back of the bell section. Pulling it out makes the whole instrument longer and lower.
- **Lock**: the nut that holds the two sections together.

**Slide section**

- **Slide braces**: two cross bars that hold the slide tubes together. Your left hand holds the first, your right hand the second.
- **Slide lock**: a small catch that keeps the slide from moving when it is not in use.
- **Water key**: the lever that lets the water out.
- **Stockings**: the slightly thicker ends of the inner slide tubes, where the slide moves against the outer tubes. They need oil (see Looking after it).

**Mouthpiece**: the **cup** you buzz into, a **shank** that fits into the **mouthpiece receiver** at the front of the slide.

### Is the trombone for you? {#selecting}

The book lists five things that help: you are **tall enough** to handle it, your **arms reach** the low positions, your lips are **medium to thick** (thin lips tend to suit trumpet and horn),
you can **sing a familiar folk song**, and your **sense of pitch** is good. These are guidelines, not tests.

## Putting it together {#assembly}

1. Hold the **slide section** by its braces in your **right hand**, with the **taller side of the slide toward you**.
2. Hold the **bell section** in your **left hand**. Put the bell section's receiver over the taller side of the slide so that the two make a **"V"**.
3. Tighten the **lock** that holds the two sections together.
4. Put the **mouthpiece** into the receiver. Twist it in gently, **not too tight**.

## Holding it {#posture}

1. Sit up straight, near the **edge of your chair**, feet flat on the floor.
2. **Left thumb** around the bell brace; **left index finger** on or near the stem of the mouthpiece.
3. The rest of your **left fingers** wrap around the **first slide brace**.
4. **Right hand** on the **second slide brace**: thumb on top, two fingers underneath.
5. Bring the trombone to your mouth, resting on your **left shoulder**.
6. **Left wrist straight**, in line with your forearm. **Right wrist loose.** **Elbows away** from your body.

## Your buzz and first note {#embouchure}

Your **embouchure** (*OM-boo-shur*) is the shape of your mouth and lips on the mouthpiece.

1. Wet your lips. Shape the inside of your mouth and throat as if saying **"oh"**, and bring your lips together as if saying **"em"**.
2. Take a full breath through your mouth and **blow through closed lips** so they make a relaxed **buzz**.
3. Hold the **mouthpiece by the shank** on its own. Put it over the middle of the buzz with **equal amounts of mouthpiece on the top and bottom lip**,
   and no heavy pressure. Check in a mirror.
4. Take a full breath and play a long, steady buzz on the mouthpiece.
5. Put the mouthpiece in the trombone and play a long, steady note in **1st position** (slide all the way in).

**Checklist** (have a friend or teacher watch): sitting straight · head up · left hand and wrist · right hand and wrist · trombone at the right angle to your body ·
fingers gently curved · elbows away from your body · mouthpiece in the right place · corners of the lips firm and the centre relaxed · chin flat and pointed · breathing properly · relaxed buzz.

## Slide positions: the chart {#slide-chart}

The slide makes the tube longer. **A longer tube sounds lower.** Each of the **seven positions** is about a **half step** lower than the one before it
(1st is the shortest tube, 7th the longest). That is the usual rule, and the chart agrees with it, though the chart itself does not state it.

Like every brass instrument, the trombone also plays several notes from one position, the **partials** of that tube. Tighter lips and faster air go up to the next
partial. In **1st position** the chart's notes are B♭2, F3, B♭3, D4, F4 and B♭4. So **a note is a slide position plus a partial**: where your arm is, and how your lips and air are set.

**Reading the number.** The chart's numbers are positions 1 to 7. A **minus** (−3) means a **shortened** position: a little closer to you than the number says.
**"or"** means a second choice for the same note (for example A♯/B♭3 is **1st or 5th**).

**Two clefs.** The first chart in the book is in **bass clef** (the note you hear). The second is the **T.C.** chart, in **treble clef**. It prints the same positions, but each note is written
**a major 9th higher than it sounds** (a B♭ treble clef part). So a low E2 in 7th position is read as F♯3 in treble clef.
Use the first box on each chart to switch between the two readings.

### Slide and listen {#glide}

Because there are no fixed steps, you can slide **between** the positions. Choose a partial, press the button, and drag the slide while the note sounds: the pitch follows your arm,
about a half step lower each time you pass a position. This is a plain physical model (position 1 is the pitch you chose, each step out lowers it by a semitone), so each position is exactly in tune here,
but a real trombone's positions are **not** equal in spacing, and the page does not claim the picture's distances are measured.

## The F attachment {#attachment}

Many tenor trombones and most bass trombones have a **rotary valve** with extra tubing, called the **F attachment**. You work it with a **trigger** under your left thumb.
(Bass trombones may have a second one, the **E attachment**.) The F attachment has two main purposes.

1. **Extra range.** With the trigger pressed the trombone switches to the **F series**: the tube is longer and its partials are those of F.
   The book's picture shows them as F1 (the **fundamental**, the lowest note and not one you normally play), F2, C3, F3, A3 and C4.
2. **Easier positions.** For students with **shorter arms**, the far positions (5th, 6th, 7th) are hard to reach. The book says some teachers recommend:
   **C (in the staff, C3)** in **1st position with the trigger** instead of 6th, and **B natural (B2)** in **2nd position with the trigger** instead of 7th.

The explorer shows those two as a third picture, labelled "with the F-attachment trigger down". The page does **not** show F-side positions for other notes: those
pages of the book were not available for this lesson (see below).

## When the tone goes wrong {#tone-problems}

| What it sounds like | Probably because… | Try this |
|---|---|---|
| **No tone, just rushing air** | Lips not firm enough | Firm up your embouchure |
| | You are blowing, not buzzing | Practise buzzing the lips without a mouthpiece |
| | Air stream blocked: closed throat, tongue too high | Think "oh" to open the throat; keep the tongue down |
| **Thin, pinched** | Lips squeezed too tight | Relax your lips; use a wider stream of air |
| | Not enough air going through | Review your breathing; use faster air |
| **Garbled** | Lips not firm enough | Firm up your embouchure |
| | Lips folding over the teeth | Re-form the embouchure; use a mouthpiece ring to check lip position |
| **Stopped, intense air** | Lips pinched completely together | Relax your lips |
| | Not enough air between the lips | Check the tongue position with "oh"; increase air speed |
| **Sharp in the upper register** | Too much pressure on the lips | Faster air, less pressure |
| **Flat, flabby low notes** | Air too slow | Use faster air |
| | Loose, flabby lips | Firm up your embouchure |
| **Hard to play high** | Air not fast enough | Increase air speed |
| **Hard to play low** | Too much pressure | Relax your lips |

## Playing in tune {#tuning}

**Good tone comes first.** To tune, play an agreed pitch **in 1st position** and move the **tuning slide**. For most instruments the tuning slide is pulled out about **¾ to 1 inch**.
The book's tuning pitches (in the bass clef) are **B♭2, then F3** for beginners, and **F3, then B♭3** for more advanced players.
Check them against a tuner (the navbar has one).

Because the slide can fine-tune any note, the trombone **does not have the built-in tuning problems of valved brass** and can play perfectly in tune. But a beginner cannot easily
**tell whether the slide is in the right place**, so good ears matter more than on any valved instrument. Sing or hum the note before you play it, and use a tuner to see how close your positions are.

- **Short arms.** Playing in tune is hardest if you cannot reach the 5th, 6th and 7th positions. An F attachment can help (see above).
- **Don't touch the bell.** The 3rd position is near the bell, and many beginners touch the bell with a finger to find it. That stops you from adjusting the slide, causes
  tuning trouble, and slows your technique. Learn to find 3rd by ear and by arm.

## Mouthpieces and mutes {#mutes}

**Mouthpieces.** A beginner should use a mouthpiece of **moderate** cup diameter, cup depth, throat and rim. As your embouchure strengthens, a larger cup is often recommended, and advanced players
pick mouthpieces to suit what they play. **Ask a trombone teacher before choosing.** The book lists (all trombone mouthpieces named by size):

| Level | Mouthpieces the book lists |
|---|---|
| Beginner | Bach 12C, 11C, 7C, 6½AL |
| Intermediate | Bach 7C, 6½AL, 5GS; Schilke 50 |
| Advanced | Bach 6½AL, 5G, 5GS, 4G; Schilke 51, 51B, 51D, 52D, 52E2 |
| Bass trombone | Bach 1¼G, 1½G, 2G, 3G; Schilke 57, 58, 59, 60 |

**Mutes** change the tone colour, and they also make the instrument **quieter**, so play a little louder to make up for it. **Most mutes make the trombone play sharp**,
especially in the **low register**. Pull the **tuning slide out** when you put a mute in, and push it back when you take the mute out. Common mutes: **straight, cup, bucket, plunger and derby**.
If the composer does not say which mute, use a **straight mute**. In a section, **everyone uses the same kind** unless the music says otherwise.

## Looking after it {#care}

**Putting it away**

1. Press the **water key** and **blow** (do not buzz) through the trombone to empty the water.
2. Wipe the trombone with a soft, clean cloth.
3. Take out the mouthpiece and put it in the case.
4. Undo the lock, take off the bell section and put it in the case.
5. Clean the slide, **lock it**, put it in the case, and latch the case.

**Oiling the slide (daily)**

1. Unlock the slide and carefully extend it until the tops of the **stockings** (the raised parts of the inner slide) show.
2. Put **5 or 6 drops of slide oil** on both stockings. A little **slide cream** works too; if you use cream, spray the slide often with water.
3. Move the slide in and out to spread the oil or cream evenly.

**Greasing the tuning slide (regularly)**

1. Take the tuning slide off. 2. Wipe off the old grease with a rag. 3. Put a **generous** amount of grease on it. 4. Put it back and move it in and out to work the grease in.
5. Push it all the way in and wipe off the extra. 6. Put it back where it was.

## What is unverified {#unverified}

Check these with your teacher.

- **Which book.** The pages come from a teacher's instrument guide (footer code "W74", the same as the saxophone lesson). The title and authors are not printed on the scanned pages, so the Works Cited says so.
- The book's pages **197 to 200 and 207 to 212** were not in the scan. That is why the **alto** and **valve** trombone, and any F-side positions beyond the book's two named alternates, are not here.
- The chart is read as **sounding pitch in bass clef**. The tenor trombone is non-transposing, and the positions agree with the usual series (each is checked on this page, so every printed position really plays that note).
- The **treble clef** chart is **B♭ treble clef** (written a major 9th above the sound). This was worked out from the printed letters (every note is two letter names higher than in the bass clef chart); the staff octave was checked against the printed ledger lines only at the two ends.
- The **partial numbers** are worked out on this page; the chart does not print them. The 7th partial is naturally a little flat, which is why the chart shortens those positions.
- How far a **shortened** position is drawn from its number is a guess (the chart only shows a minus sign). The chart prints **G♯4 as "−3"**, like F♯4; by the series that is a 3rd position note and needs no shortening, but the page keeps what is printed.
- The **distances between positions in the drawing** are the teacher's drawing, not measured on an instrument.
- That a position is about a half step from its neighbours is a standard fact (see Works Cited), not printed on the chart.
- The sound is a synthesized buzz, not a recording of a trombone.
